```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`answer_document()` asks one question of one document. Most real work has a
folder of them, and a literature review has a folder, a search behind it, and a
write-up at the end that somebody else has to be able to check. This guide
covers that work in the order it happens:

1. Asking one question of every document, with `gr_read_many()`.
2. Starting a review from a database search, with `gr_search()` and
   `gr_records()`.
3. The review itself: one trace for every stage, `gr_protocol()`, then
   `gr_screen()`, measuring the screening against a person with
   `gr_reference()` and `gr_calibrate()` (recall against a target, when
   ranked screening can stop, several reviewers), then `gr_extract()` and its
   agreement with a person's table, and `gr_synthesise()`.
4. Writing from claims instead of from rows, with `gr_claims()`,
   `gr_outline()` and `gr_gaps()`.
5. Counting and reporting the whole run, with `gr_flow()` and
   `gr_audit_report()`.

`vignette("harnessr")` introduces the package and its ideas, and how one
document is read is in `vignette("readers")`. Read `vignette("runs")` first if
you have not set spending limits or a cache: this guide points to it for both,
and for replay.
Comparing whole configurations on a labelled set of questions, with intervals,
is in `vignette("evaluate")`.

## Setting up

Everything below runs offline. `gr_mock_client()` stands in for the model: its
handler is an ordinary R function. `embedder = "lexical"` keeps retrieval free
and deterministic.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")
cl <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
```

## Reading many documents

Before reading a folder you have not read before, `gr_inventory()` lists what is
in it: which extractor reads each file, which have no text layer and which would
be skipped, with no model calls and no key. `vignette("ingest")` shows it on a
folder and covers what to do about files with no extractor or no text layer.

`gr_compare()` runs several recipes over one document. `gr_read_many()` runs one
recipe over many, and returns one row per document. That is the shape the work
usually has: a folder, one question, and a table at the end.

```{r}
reports <- file.path(tempdir(), "reports")
dir.create(reports, showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines("Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024.", file.path(reports, "north.txt"))
writeLines("Revenue was 51.8 million dollars in fiscal 2025.", file.path(reports, "south.txt"))

out <- gr_read_many(reports, "What was revenue?", "fast", client = cl)
out$summary[, c("document", "not_found", "chunks_used", "calls", "status")]
```

A directory is expanded by the extractor registry, so registering an extractor
changes which files get picked up. A document keeps the folder it came from, so
`2019/report.txt` and `2020/report.txt` stay distinguishable instead of
collapsing to one name. The full summary also carries `answer`, `partial`,
`reader`, `chunks`, `cached`, `tokens_in`, `tokens_out`, `cost_usd`, `seconds`
and `error`, and `write.csv(out$summary, ...)` is a reasonable end to a run.

`gr_read_many()` does five things a `lapply()` does not.

One bad file costs one row. An unreadable document gets `status = "failed"`
and its error in the `error` column, and the other hundred and ninety-nine
answers survive. Pass `on_error = "stop"` if you would rather it aborted.

Budgets are per document, and the run has its own. Every document gets its
own trace, so `gr_options(max_calls =)` and `gr_options(max_cost_usd =)` apply to
each one exactly as if you had read it alone, and one enormous document cannot
starve the rest. On its own that leaves the run unbounded: two hundred documents
under a 400-call ceiling is a corpus ceiling of eighty thousand calls. So there
are two run-level ceilings.

```{r}
out <- gr_read_many(reports, "What was revenue?", "fast", client = cl,
                    max_total_calls = 2000,   # checked BEFORE each document
                    max_total_usd   = 20)     # checked after each one
```

`max_total_calls` is checked before a document, so the overshoot is bounded by
one document's own ceiling. `max_total_usd` can only be checked after one, since
what a document costs is not knowable until it has been read. It also needs a
model with a registered price, or cost is unknown rather than zero and you get a
`gr_corpus_cost_unknown` warning instead of a silent free pass. Documents past
either ceiling are marked `"skipped"` rather than dropped. Set neither and the
run says once what its worst case is. `gr_screen()` and `gr_extract()` take the
same two arguments.

A run can be resumed. Point `store =` at a directory and each result is
written as it completes and restored on a later run. Combined with a durable
response cache, restarting a four-hour job costs approximately nothing:

```{r eval = FALSE}
durable <- gr_cache_client(cl, gr_cache(tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache")))
gr_read_many(reports, "What was revenue?", "thorough",
             client = durable, store = file.path(tempdir(), "run-store"))
```

The store is keyed on the document's path, size and mtime, the question, the
whole pipeline and the model, so an edited document is a new job, not a stale
hit. A `gr_backend_client()` needs a stable `id` for a store or a cache to be
reused by a later session; `gr_client()` and `gr_ellmer_client()` already know
what they are.

The same document is read once. The same paper reaches you from three
databases under three filenames. A source whose cleaned text repeats one already
read is not read again: its row is filled in from the first copy, `status` is
`"duplicate"`, and `duplicate_of` names the row it repeats. Every source you
passed still has a row, so `subset(out$summary, is.na(duplicate_of))` is the
deduplicated set and `sum(!is.na(out$summary$duplicate_of))` is the number to
report as removed. A response cache already made the second copy's calls free;
what it could not do was stop the duplicate appearing in the results as a
second, independent document.

`document_id`, beside `document` in the summary, is the hash of that cleaned
text. Cite with it. A filename changes when the file is renamed, collides
between folders, and does not exist at all for a document passed as text, while
the id is the same string for the same document in every run and on every
machine.

You can see what it cost. `out$trace` holds the run's calls, and
`gr_trace_cost()` prices them at each step's own model, counting only the calls
that were issued. The mock client has no price, so this bill is zero;
`vignette("runs")` explains the columns and how to register a price.

```{r}
gr_trace_cost(out$trace)[, c("model", "calls", "paid_calls", "usd")]
```

## From a search to a review

A folder of PDFs cannot say which databases were searched, with what query, on
what date, or how many records came back, and no care further down substitutes
for that. `gr_search()` records the search, and `gr_records()` reads the export
your reference manager already produces (RIS here):

```{r}
search <- gr_search(
  databases = c(PubMed = "(spaced practice[tiab]) AND (retention[tiab])",
                Scopus = 'TITLE-ABS-KEY("spaced practice" AND retention)'),
  dates = "2026-02-14",
  limits = "English; 2000 onwards; primary studies only",
  registration = "PROSPERO CRD42026000000"
)

# Two exports of the same corpus, as two databases would give them.
exports <- file.path(tempdir(), "exports"); dir.create(exports, showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines(c("TY  - JOUR", "AU  - Smith, J.", "AU  - Okafor, A.",
             "TI  - Cognitive load and retention", "PY  - 2019",
             "DO  - https://doi.org/10.1037/EDU0000123", "DB  - Scopus", "ER  - ",
             "TY  - JOUR", "AU  - Gone, G.", "TI  - Never obtained", "PY  - 2020",
             "DO  - 10.1000/zzz", "DB  - Scopus", "ER  - "),
           file.path(exports, "scopus.ris"))
writeLines(c("TY  - JOUR", "AU  - Smith J", "TI  - Cognitive Load and Retention.",
             "DP  - 2019 Mar", "DO  - 10.1037/edu0000123", "ER  -"),
           file.path(exports, "pubmed.ris"))

pdfs <- file.path(tempdir(), "pdfs"); dir.create(pdfs, showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines("A randomised trial of spacing.", file.path(pdfs, "smith2019.txt"))

recs <- gr_records(exports, files = pdfs, search = search)
recs
```

Hand `recs` to `gr_screen()` and `gr_extract()` wherever you would have passed a
folder. Four things follow from it that a folder cannot give you.

The flow counts start at identification. `gr_flow()` begins at records
identified rather than at "sources given", which is already past the step that
decides whether anyone can reproduce the search.

Records with no document stay visible. Fourteen reports sought and not retrieved
is a finding about the review, and a folder represents it as nothing at all.

Duplicates are settled by DOI, not by text. The same paper from three databases
is one record, and `duplicate_of` names the row each one repeats. Where a DOI is
missing (preprints, conference papers), normalised title and year are the
fallback, but two records that both have DOIs and differ are never merged,
because similar titles happen and merging two studies is the error this whole
path exists to avoid.

Authors and years become facts. `gr_synthesise()` cites by name, and without an
export those names came from asking a model to read a title page. That is the one
part of a citation that must be exactly right, resting on the loosest guarantee
in the pipeline. From an export they are data, joined onto the extraction table,
and the model is still never shown them.

Matching records to files uses the path the export recorded, then the DOI in the
filename, then the title, then first-author surname and year, which is how
people name downloads. An ambiguous match is no match: two Smith 2019 papers and
one `smith2019.pdf` claim nothing, because a coin flip presented as a match is
how one paper's findings get attributed to another.

## The review: protocol, screen, extract, write

The single-document pipeline (ingest, segment, read) answers a question. A
corpus job usually wants a table, and a review wants a table plus the account of
it. Four functions cover that, and they compose in one direction:

`gr_protocol()` → `gr_screen()` → `gr_extract()` → `gr_synthesise()`

### One trace for the whole review

Passing the same `trace =` to `gr_screen()`, `gr_extract()`, `gr_claims()`,
`gr_outline()` and `gr_synthesise()` accumulates the whole review in one place.
It is a parent: each stage still records on a trace of its own, which is what
its `$trace` returns and what `gr_options(max_calls =)` is measured against, and
adds its calls to the shared one when it finishes. So the screening cannot spend
the write-up's ceiling, the shared trace's totals are the sum of the stages',
and each request is counted once.

`gr_outline()` records its calls on `attr(outline, "trace")`, which
`gr_outline_pick()` keeps and `gr_synthesise()` keeps as `$outline_trace`; it
does not add them to `claims$trace`. To total a review's cost, pass one trace to
every stage, or add `attr(outline, "trace")` to the claims' own.

### The protocol

A protocol is what you fix before reading anything: which documents count, what
to collect from the ones that do, and what the write-up has to cover. Fixing it
first matters because a criterion invented while reading is a criterion fitted
to what was found.

```{r}
protocol <- gr_protocol(
  "revenue-review",
  question = "How did revenue change across the regional reports?",
  include  = "Reports a revenue figure",
  exclude  = "Is a forecast rather than a result",
  fields   = gr_fields(
    region  = "The region the report covers",
    revenue = gr_field("Revenue in millions of dollars", type = "number"),
    year    = gr_field("Fiscal year reported", type = "integer")
  ),
  outline  = c("Findings" = "How revenue compares across regions")
)
protocol
```

`gr_protocols()` lists four templates to start from: `bibliography`, `claims`,
`evidence_table` and `systematic_review`. `gr_protocol_save()` and
`gr_protocol_read()` round-trip a protocol through a JSON file, so it can be
shared, diffed and cited alongside the results.

### Screening

Screening is one call per document, and nothing is dropped. Every document gets
a decision and a reason. There is no retrieval step that could quietly remove a
source before one is recorded. A file that could not be read gets
`status = "failed"` and no decision rather than a silent exclusion, and
`"unclear"` is an answer rather than a forced guess, because forcing a binary
call on an excerpt that does not settle it is how automated screening loses
studies.

This stand-in screener includes the northern report and cannot decide about the
southern one:

```{r}
screener <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  seen <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) as.character(m$content), character(1)),
                collapse = " ")
  if (grepl("51.8", seen, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return('{"decision":"unclear","reason":"The excerpt does not say whether this is a result.",
             "criterion":null,"quote":null}')
  }
  line <- regmatches(seen, regexpr("Revenue was [0-9.]+ million dollars in fiscal [0-9]+\\.", seen))
  sprintf('{"decision":"include","reason":"Reports a revenue figure.",
            "criterion":"Reports a revenue figure","quote":"%s"}', line)
})

screened <- gr_screen(reports, protocol, client = screener)
screened$table[, c("document", "decision", "criterion", "verified")]
```

The reply must fit the schema the request sent. A decision outside `include`,
`exclude` and `unclear` is a failed call, not a guess at what the model meant,
and it is not cached, so running again asks again.

`screened$forward` holds the included and unclear records, the set to read at
full text, and `screened$deferred` holds the unclear ones, for a person to
settle:

```{r}
basename(screened$forward)
basename(screened$deferred)
```

`gr_resolve()` records that person's decision. It needs to know who decided, and
it records when (in UTC) and, optionally, why, in the table and as a
`"screen.resolve"` step in the trace. `forward`, `deferred` and `included` are
rebuilt, and the screener's own decision is kept in `screener_decision`:

```{r}
screened <- gr_resolve(screened, "south.txt", "include", by = "A. Reviewer",
                       reason = "The report covers fiscal 2025 actuals.")
screened$table[, c("document", "decision", "screener_decision", "resolved_by")]
```

`gr_calibrate()` compares against `screener_decision`, so a person's correction
is not credited to the screener. Duplicates of a resolved record take the same
decision.

Hand `screened` itself to `gr_extract()`. In this release that reads the
included records only, and warns (class `gr_unclear_dropped`) when it leaves
unclear ones out; from the next release it reads `$forward`. Pass
`screened$forward` to read the unclear records now. `screened$included` works
too, but a character vector of paths cannot carry the search forward, so the
audit's search section and the bibliographic columns are lost with it.
`table(screened$table$criterion)` is the breakdown a flow diagram asks for.

### Knowing how good the screening is

`gr_screen()` gives every document a decision. Nothing in the run says whether
those decisions were any good, and a screener that discards a fifth of the
eligible studies produces a carefully audited review of the wrong corpus.

The tempting substitute is running the model twice and reporting the agreement.
It measures the wrong thing: two passes share weights, priors and blind spots,
so they agree most confidently where they are both wrong. Only a reference
standard settles it. `gr_reference()` draws a sample for a person to screen by
hand, and `gr_calibrate()` compares the two.

```{r}
# A screening run: 340 discarded, 72 kept.
big <- structure(list(table = data.frame(
  document = sprintf("rec%03d.pdf", 1:412),
  decision = c(rep("exclude", 340), rep("include", 60), rep("unclear", 12)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)), class = "gr_screening")

# Sample what it threw away: that is where a permanent loss hides.
check <- gr_reference(big, n = 60, of = "excluded", seed = 1)

# ... a person fills in `human_decision`, blind to what the model said.
check$human_decision <- c(rep("exclude", 57), rep("include", 3))

gr_calibrate(big, check)
```

Which rows you sample changes which questions the sample can answer. A sample
of exclusions contains no kept records, so sensitivity would compute to 0% and
specificity to 100%. Both are artifacts of the frame, alarming or flattering,
and neither is a fact about the screener, so `gr_calibrate()` reports what the
frame supports and refuses the rest. The frame travels as a column in the CSV,
because that file gets emailed, opened in Excel and read back a fortnight later,
and an attribute survives none of that. In a blind sheet the column is an opaque
key, so the person filling it in cannot tell from it what the model decided, and
the CSV is UTF-8 with a byte-order mark so Excel opens accented names intact.

A sample drawn from everything screened (`of = "all"`) supports the rest. This
one is the eight-record example from `?gr_calibrate`:

```{r}
tab <- data.frame(document = paste0("d", 1:8, ".pdf"),
                  decision = c("include", "include", "unclear", "exclude",
                               "exclude", "exclude", "include", "exclude"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ref <- data.frame(document = paste0("d", 1:8, ".pdf"),
                  human_decision = c("include", "exclude", "include", "exclude",
                                     "exclude", "include", "include", "exclude"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cal <- gr_calibrate(structure(list(table = tab), class = "gr_screening"), ref,
                    of = "all")
cal
```

`"unclear"` counts as a deferral to a person, not as a miss, because a record
the screener could not settle goes to a person, and counting it as a failure
would punish the one behaviour that makes it safe. Two sensitivities are
reported. Sensitivity as deployed is the share of eligible studies that were
kept, by `"include"` or by `"unclear"`, and is the one where a shortfall is
permanent. Strict sensitivity is the share actively included. The gap between
them is the reading you still have to do. The rate of `"unclear"` decisions is
the "deferred to a person" line, with its interval, and `cal$decisions` holds
the 3x2 counts behind it all.

Accuracy is not reported, and kappa is not reported alone. At a realistic
inclusion rate a screener that excluded everything scores about 95% accurate
and finds nothing. Agreement is taken on the same decision sensitivity uses,
kept (include or unclear) against excluded, in `cal$agreement$kept`, with strict
include against the rest beside it in `cal$agreement$strict`. Each table gives
Cohen's kappa next to PABAK and Gwet's AC1, with intervals, the prevalence and
bias indices, and the class-wise sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV, because
at a few eligible records in a hundred kappa moves with prevalence as much as
with agreement:

```{r}
cal$agreement$kept$stats
```

`cal$agreement$kept$paradox` is `TRUE` when the prevalence index is above 0.8 in
absolute value, where kappa says more about prevalence than about agreement. The
kappa interval is a percentile bootstrap over documents, B = 2000, under a fixed
seed, so the same sample gives the same interval and the session's random stream
is untouched; `cal$agreement$kept$bootstrap` holds B and the seed. AC1 uses
Gwet's (2008) variance. Where the screener and the person agree on every record,
disagree on every record, or the sample holds fewer than 10 records, as here,
the kappa and AC1 intervals are left empty with a `note` saying why, instead of
a zero-width interval such as [1.00, 1.00].

Before this release kappa was taken over the screener's three labels against
the person's two, so every `"unclear"` counted as a disagreement. On this
example that gave 0.33 where the kept-against-excluded figure is 0.50. The old
figure is `cal$kappa_legacy` for this release only, and is removed in the next.

A rate from three observations is not a finding. The intervals on the rates are
Wilson score intervals, which stay sensible at zero and one where the textbook
interval collapses to a point, and `$adequate` says when the sample cannot
support a claim. What is enough depends on the frame: enough eligible studies
for sensitivity in a sample of everything screened (`min_positives`, 10 by
default), and for a sample of one stratum (exclusions, or kept records) an
interval no wider than 10 points, or the whole stratum judged. `$missed` is the
list of studies the screener discarded and a person did not, which is usually
more use than any rate.

Pass the result to `gr_audit_report(calibration = )` and it becomes a section of
the report, with the 3x2 counts and every statistic above, so the figure a
reviewer asks for sits next to the run it describes instead of being copied
into a methods section by hand.

### Recall against a target

Sensitivity as deployed is recall: the share of eligible studies the screener
kept. A review usually sets a target for it, such as 95%, and the claim worth
making is that recall is at least the target, at a stated confidence. A sample
of the exclusions alone cannot support that claim, because it counts none of
the eligible records that were kept. The design that can is the one people use
anyway: judge every record the screener kept, and a sample of what it excluded.
`of = "stacked"` draws both in one sheet.

The target fixes how many exclusions to judge. Recall is K / (K + M), with K
the eligible records kept and M the eligible records excluded, so a target is
a cap on M. If a pilot suggests about 50 of the 72 kept records are eligible,
95% recall allows floor(50 x 0.05 / 0.95) = 2 of them to have been lost.
`gr_screen_sample_size()` gives the number of the 340 exclusions to judge so
that, if none of them turns out eligible, the bound on M is 2:

```{r}
gr_screen_sample_size(frame = "stacked", max_lost = 2,
                      frame_n = 340)[, c("frame", "max_lost", "frame_n", "n", "n_binomial")]
```

215 is the exact size from the hypergeometric distribution of a frame of 340
records; the binomial rule, which ignores that the frame is finite, asks for
508. For a sample of everything screened (`frame = "all"`) the rule is
k >= ln(alpha) / ln(T) eligible records with no miss: 59 for 95% recall at 95%
confidence, which at 5% prevalence means drawing 1180 records, or 388 from a
frame of 500:

```{r}
gr_screen_sample_size(0.95, 0.95, prevalence = 0.05,
                      frame_n = 500)[, c("positives", "n", "n_binomial")]
```

So draw every kept record and 215 of the exclusions:

```{r}
stacked <- gr_reference(big, n = 215, of = "stacked", seed = 1)
nrow(stacked)

# ... a person judges every row, blind. Here 50 of the 72 kept records are
# eligible, and none of the 215 sampled exclusions.
kept <- big$table$decision[match(stacked$document, big$table$document)] != "exclude"
stacked$human_decision <- "exclude"
stacked$human_decision[which(kept)[1:50]] <- "include"

recall <- gr_calibrate(big, stacked)
unlist(recall$recall[c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "bound")])
unlist(recall$lost[c("estimate", "bound", "frame_n")])
recall$verdict$met
```

Each stratum is weighted by how much of it was judged: all 72 kept records
count once, and each of the 215 sampled exclusions stands for 340 / 215 of
them. Recall is the ratio of the weighted (Horvitz-Thompson) totals, from
`hr_ht_estimate()`. M is bounded exactly from the hypergeometric distribution
of what the sample found, and the one-sided lower bound on recall is
K / (K + M_U), here 50 / 52 = 0.962, above the target. No bootstrap is used:
with no eligible record in the sample every resample also finds none, and the
interval would be [1, 1].

One eligible record among the sampled exclusions is enough to miss the target.
It stands for 340 / 215 records, and the bound has to allow for more than that:

```{r}
one_miss <- stacked
one_miss$human_decision[which(!kept)[1]] <- "include"
missed <- gr_calibrate(big, one_miss)
round(missed$recall$bound, 3)
missed$verdict$met
```

A blind stacked sheet keeps each row's stratum and inclusion probability inside
its `sampled_from` key, one key per row, and lists the rows in the run's order
rather than by stratum, so the person filling it in cannot tell which records
the screener kept. A kept sheet and an excluded sheet drawn separately and
joined with `rbind()` are read the same way with `gr_calibrate(of =
"stacked")`. On a stacked reference the result also has `lost` (M with its
bounds), `false_exclusion`, `work_saved`, `unclear_rate`, `strata` and
`verdict`; agreement statistics are left out there, since unweighted they would
be distorted the same way unweighted sensitivity is.

### When prioritised screening can stop

`gr_screen()` reads every record once, so it has no stopping point to choose.
Screening that reads records in ranked order, most likely relevant first, does:
after enough irrelevant records in a row, the rest are probably irrelevant too.
`gr_stop_test()` makes that a test. After each screened record it gives the
p-value for recall still being below `target`, given how many records are
left, and the first point where screening may stop at `alpha` (Callaghan and
Muller-Hansen 2020). Here 1,000 records are screened in ranked order: the first
100 are relevant, the next 400 are not, and 500 are unread:

```{r}
seen <- c(rep(1, 100), rep(0, 400), rep(NA, 500))
gr_stop_test(seen)
```

The test treats the last records screened as a random draw from those left,
which a ranking is not: when the ranker works it is cautious, and when it ranks
worse than chance it cannot be trusted. Nor is it corrected for looking after
every record. Report the rule and its settings with the result.
`hr_baseline_ranker()` simulates such an order with a cheap model and no calls,
and `gr_stop_test()` accepts its result; `vignette("evaluate")` shows it.

### Several reviewers

One person's decisions are a reference, but not a perfect one, and how far two
people agree is the yardstick for how far a screener agrees with either.
`gr_reference(reviewers = k)` writes one decision column per reviewer and a
`consensus` column for an adjudicator:

```{r}
pair <- gr_reference(big, n = 40, of = "all", seed = 2, reviewers = 2)
names(pair)

# ... two people screen the 40 records; the second includes three records the
# first excluded.
eligible <- big$table$decision[match(pair$document, big$table$document)] != "exclude"
pair$human_decision_1 <- ifelse(eligible, "include", "exclude")
pair$human_decision_2 <- pair$human_decision_1
pair$human_decision_2[c(3, 11, 25)] <- "include"
```

`gr_calibrate()` compares the screener with the reviewers' consensus, and it
will not guess one: a disagreement nobody settled stops it, saying how many
there were.

```{r}
tryCatch(gr_calibrate(big, pair), error = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e)))
```

`gr_reference_consensus()` forms one decision per document by a rule.
`"majority"` takes the decision of more than half the reviewers, and settles a
tie by the `consensus` column where it is filled and otherwise as include, so a
reference never excludes a record half its reviewers included. With two
reviewers every disagreement is a tie. `"any_include"` carries a record forward
unless every reviewer excluded it, and `"adjudicated"` takes the `consensus`
column and stops where it is empty. `consensus_from` says how each row's
decision was reached:

```{r}
table(gr_reference_consensus(pair, "majority")$consensus_from)
```

Here an adjudicator settles the three instead, and the calibration runs:

```{r}
pair$consensus[c(3, 11, 25)] <- "exclude"
both <- gr_calibrate(big, pair)
both$reviewers$agreement[, c("statistic", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
both$reviewers$sensitivity[, c("reviewer", "statistic", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "n")]
```

`$reviewers` gives every pair of reviewers the observed agreement, kappa,
PABAK, AC1 and the prevalence and bias indices from `hr_agreement()`, never
kappa alone, and Krippendorff's alpha over all of them with three reviewers or
more. It also gives each reviewer's sensitivity and specificity against the
consensus, which says what one person screening alone would have missed. Each
reviewer is part of the consensus they are scored against, so these figures
run higher than against an independent reference, the more so with fewer
reviewers. On a stacked reference both are weighted the way recall is.

### Extraction

Extraction fills the protocol's fields from every chunk of each included
document, then reconciles them. The result is one typed row per document, and
every filled cell carries the sentence it came from, checked against the chunk
it was attributed to. A paragraph about one paper cannot be compared with a
paragraph about two hundred others; a table can be sorted, counted, filtered and
published.

```{r}
extractor <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  seen <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) as.character(m$content), character(1)),
                collapse = " ")
  n <- if (grepl("45.2", seen, fixed = TRUE)) "45.2" else "51.8"
  yr <- if (grepl("2024", seen, fixed = TRUE)) 2024 else 2025
  rg <- if (grepl("45.2", seen, fixed = TRUE)) "north" else "south"
  line <- sprintf("Revenue was %s million dollars in fiscal %d.", n, yr)
  sprintf('{"region":"%s","revenue":%s,"year":%d,
            "region__quote":"%s","revenue__quote":"%s","year__quote":"%s"}',
          rg, n, yr, line, line, line)
})

table <- gr_extract(screened, protocol, client = extractor, recipe = "fast")
table$table[, c("document", "region", "revenue", "year", "n_unverified")]
```

Reconciling the chunks costs nothing by default. Where the document contradicts
itself, `conflicts` names the field and the earliest chunk's value is kept;
`resolve = "model"` spends one call per disagreeing field to have the model
choose instead.

`n_unverified` is the column to look at before believing a row: zero means every
value in it can be pointed at in the document. `table$evidence` is the long
form, one row per supported cell, with the quote, the page it is on, and whether
the quote appears there.

```{r}
table$evidence[, c("document_id", "field", "quote", "verified")]
```

Nothing is discarded for failing that check; `require_quote = TRUE` makes
discarding a choice rather than a surprise. A value is read by its field's type,
so "1,204" in an integer field is 1204, and a value the field does not allow is
reported as one it could not read.

### Agreement on extracted fields

`n_unverified` says whether a value can be found in the document, not whether
it is the value a person would have taken. For that, have a person fill the
same fields for a sample of documents (`gr_label_sheet("extraction", ...)`
writes the sheet; `vignette("evaluate")` shows how sheets are read back) and
compare the tables with `gr_extract_agreement()`. It matches rows on
`document` and compares each field on its own, with Krippendorff's alpha at the
field's level of measurement: interval for `integer` and `number` fields and
nominal otherwise, unless `levels =` names another. Here a model and a person
extracted two fields from 40 studies:

```{r}
fields <- gr_fields(
  design = gr_field("Study design", type = "enum", values = c("rct", "cohort", "case series")),
  n      = gr_field("Number randomised", type = "integer"))

studies_40 <- sprintf("s%02d.pdf", 1:40)
person <- data.frame(document = studies_40,
                     design = rep(c("rct", "cohort", "rct", "case series"), 10),
                     n = 30 + 7 * (1:40))
person$n[c(5, 30)] <- NA
model <- person
model$design[c(4, 17)] <- c("rct", "cohort")
model$n[c(9, 22, 31)] <- c(94, NA, 58)

ag <- gr_extract_agreement(model, person, fields = fields, B = 200)
ag
subset(ag$pairs, x != y)
```

A blank, `NA` or "not reported" cell means the document does not report the
field. In a nominal field that is one more category. A numeric field cannot
place it on its scale, so it gets two rows: whether the field is reported at
all, and the value where both tables report it. Alpha at the interval level
gives partial credit for a near miss, so 94 against 93 costs far less than 58
against 247, while percent agreement counts both as disagreements. Below 30
documents, or for a field that never varies, alpha is `NA` and a note says why;
read percent agreement there. A `gr_extract()` result can be passed directly.
A row that failed is left out of every field, and an empty cell in a row read
only in part is left out rather than taken as not reported, so a document is
never counted as reporting nothing because it was not read.

### The write-up

`gr_synthesise()` makes one call per section of the outline, and every section
cites the rows it rests on:

```{r}
writer <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  paste("Revenue was higher in the southern region, at 51.8 million dollars [study 2],",
        "than in the northern, at 45.2 million [study 1].")
})

review <- gr_synthesise(table, protocol, client = writer)
review$citations
cat(review$text_marked)
```

`review$text_marked` is the text as the model wrote it, with its markers;
`review$text` is the same with the citations rendered, which the next section
covers. `review$citations` resolves each `[study n]` to its `document` and
`document_id`. The markers are parsed back out and checked against the rows that
exist; one pointing at a row that is not there is reported and marks the section
partial. Duplicates never reach the write-up, so no study is counted twice.

The citation check says which rows a sentence rests on, not what it says they
found, and the figures are what a reader copies out of a review. So every number
in the write-up is also looked for in the rows its sentence cites, as the writer
was shown them:

```{r}
review$sections[, c("section", "n_cited", "n_unbacked")]
review$figures[, c("number", "studies", "backed", "basis")]
```

The check forgives form, such as `.61` for 0.61 or `1204` for 1,204, but not a
changed digit. A figure found nowhere, such as 54.2 written for 45.2, has
`backed = FALSE`, is counted in `n_unbacked` and is warned about. It does not
make the section partial, which is about citations. A figure the cited row
carries was copied correctly, and it can still be the wrong figure for the
sentence.

### Citations a reader can use

The model writes and the package checks `[study 2]` markers; extract the
bibliographic fields alongside your own and they render as citations, with a
reference list built from the studies the finished text cites. `cite_style =
"auto"`, the default, names the studies when the table can name all of them;
`"author-year"` asks for names and warns if they cannot be produced, `"numeric"`
gives `(1, 2)`, and `"marker"` leaves `[study 1]` as written. A protocol for
that adds the bibliographic fields:

```{r eval = FALSE}
protocol <- gr_protocol(
  "spacing-review",
  question = "Does spaced practice improve retention in adult learners?",
  include  = "A primary study comparing spaced with massed practice",
  fields   = gr_fields(
    authors = "All authors, surname first",
    year    = gr_field("Year of publication", type = "integer"),
    title   = "Article title",
    venue   = "Journal, volume and issue",
    design  = "Study design",
    effect  = "Effect size with its interval"
  ),
  outline  = c("Included studies" = "How many, of what designs",
               "Findings"         = "The effect, and where studies disagree")
)
```

`gr_synthesise()` takes the extraction table, so the shape it needs is easy to
show directly:

```{r}
studies <- data.frame(
  document = c("smith.pdf", "lee.pdf", "garcia.pdf"),
  status = "ok", duplicate_of = NA_character_, n_filled = 4L,
  authors = c("Smith, J., Okafor, A.", "Lee, M., Petrov, K.", "Garcia, R."),
  year    = c(2019L, 2021L, 2022L),
  title   = c("Cognitive Load and Retention in Adult Learners",
              "Spacing Effects in Online Instruction",
              "No Effect of Spacing on Procedural Skill Acquisition"),
  venue   = c("Journal of Educational Psychology 44(2)",
              "Learning and Instruction 61(4)",
              "Applied Cognitive Psychology 36(1)"),
  effect  = c("d = 0.61", "d = 0.22", "d = 0.04"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

cite_writer <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params)
  "Three studies met the criteria [study 1] [study 2] [study 3].")

cited <- gr_synthesise(
  studies, question = "Does spaced practice improve retention?",
  outline = c("Included studies" = "How many, of what designs"),
  client  = cite_writer,
  style   = "formal academic; hedge claims; past tense for findings"
)
cat(cited$text)
```

The model still writes `[study 3]`. Rendering happens afterwards, from the
table, so a citation in the finished prose is a fact about the extraction rather
than something the model asserted. Verifying "Smith & Okafor (2019)" would mean
matching a name the model wrote against a name in the table, and the near-misses
(Smith for Smyth, 2019 for 2018) are the errors that matter and also the ones
fuzzy matching forgives. `cited$text_marked` keeps the marker form, so the check
can be re-run on what you published.

A study it cannot name makes the whole review fall back to markers. Citing some
studies by name and others by number reads as a mistake, and inventing "n.d."
would assert something the extraction never found. Ask for a `citation` field
directly if your sources are awkward; parsing an arbitrary author list is a
heuristic and is treated as one.

### Revision passes

Sections are written independently, which keeps each one answerable to its own
brief, so nothing joins them: terms drift, a study gets introduced twice, there
are no transitions. `coherence = TRUE` adds three revision passes over the
finished draft: `"structure"` reorders and merges, `"cut"` removes repetition,
and `"register"` polishes sentences. Each is forbidden from doing the others'
job, and each is a call, so they are off by default. Name a subset if you want
fewer: `coherence = "cut"`.

A revision pass may reorganise prose. It may not make the review claim more than
the draft did. The passes are the one step that could quietly undo everything
above them, so their output is checked rather than trusted, and a pass that
fails a check is discarded, leaving `review$draft`, the text from before the
passes.

A revision that added or lost a citation is discarded. That check is necessary
and not sufficient, because the most damaging thing an editing pass does leaves
the citations exactly where they were: editing for impact means deleting hedges,
and the hedges are where the uncertainty lives. "Three small trials suggest a
modest benefit" comes back as "trials show a benefit", with the same markers and
studies and a claim the evidence does not carry. So a revision is also discarded
if it introduces a universal quantifier that was not there, uses a booster
("demonstrates", "establishes", "confirms") more often than the draft did, or
carries fewer hedges than the draft's rate implies.

All three are matched on whole words. As bare substrings, "improved" counted as
an instance of "prove", so a draft saying "outcomes improved" licensed a
revision saying "proves the drug works", and a revision that added the hedge
"unproven" was rejected for introducing a booster. Boosters are counted rather
than merely listed, so saying "demonstrates" three times where the draft said it
once is introducing it.

The hedge test scales with how much claim-bearing prose survived, so a shorter
revision may carry fewer hedges, but never none if the draft had any. It does
not promise that every legitimate cut passes: a pass that removes the most
heavily hedged sentence lowers the rate and is refused. The cost of that is a
discarded pass and a warning; the draft stands.

Hedges and universal quantifiers are measured on sentences carrying a citation,
because headings, framing and transitions are exactly what an editing pass
should be free to rewrite, and "the evidence, all of which is relevant" is not a
claim. Boosters are measured on all of the prose except headings, because there
is no register in which an editing pass should introduce "demonstrates" into a
review at all, and the uncited framing between the claims is where such a
sentence gets written.

Two more checks need no model call. A `cut` pass that did not shorten the review
is discarded, since a cut that cut nothing was a polish under the wrong name. And
a revision pass that writes a figure its draft did not have, or changes which
studies are cited, is discarded; the figure check runs on the draft and again on
the revised text. `review$coherence` has one row per pass: what ran, whether it
was kept and why not, with `words_before` and `words_after`, so a pass that
halved the review can be seen.

## Writing from claims instead of from rows

The write-up above was drafted from the whole table, one section at a time, and
the prose shows it: the model goes row by row. "Smith (2019) found X. Garcia
(2022) found Y." That enumeration is a common sign of a weak review, and
it follows directly from what the prompt holds. The structure has the same
problem. The outline was fixed before anything was read, so the shape of the
review is your hypothesis, when often the strongest thing a review has to say is
structural: that a literature splits into three incompatible measures, and that
the argument about effect size is an argument about measurement.

`gr_claims()` computes the relations between studies first. Each claim names the
studies that support it, the studies that contradict it, and the field that
distinguishes them. The stand-in below plays all three stages that follow:

```{r}
claim_writer <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  sys <- messages[[1]]$content
  if (grepl("turn a table of studies", sys, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return(paste0('{"claims":[{"claim":"Revenue is higher in the south than the north.",',
                  '"kind":"finding","supported_by":[2],"contradicted_by":[1],',
                  '"moderator":"region","scope":"one report per region"},',
                  '{"claim":"The northern region reported for fiscal 2024.",',
                  '"kind":"finding","supported_by":[1],"contradicted_by":[],',
                  '"moderator":null,"scope":"one report"}]}'))
  }
  # Asked for a second outline (see below), it groups the claims another way.
  if (grepl("<earlier_outlines>", messages[[length(messages)]]$content, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return(paste0('{"sections":[{"heading":"The comparison","brief":"south against ',
                  'north","claims":[1],"rationale":"findings"},{"heading":"The reports",',
                  '"brief":"what each covers","claims":[2],"rationale":"coverage"}]}'))
  }
  if (grepl("sections of a review", sys, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return(paste0('{"sections":[{"heading":"Where revenue is higher","brief":"the ',
                  'regional comparison","claims":[1,2],"rationale":"one comparison"}]}'))
  }
  "Revenue was higher in the south [study 2] than in the north [study 1]."
})

cm <- gr_claims(table, question = protocol$question, client = claim_writer)
cm$claims[, c("claim", "moderator", "n_support", "n_contradict")]
```

`cm$support` is the long form (`claim_id`, `study`, `role`); join it to the
extraction to reach documents and quotes. Every study number in it was checked
against the table, the same check the `[study n]` markers in finished prose get,
one link earlier. A number that is not in the table is dropped and counted. A
claim left with no supporting study is dropped entirely, because a claim
attached to nothing is an opinion. A `moderator` naming a column the table does
not have is cleared, because an invented explanation for a real disagreement is
the most convincing error this layer can make. `cm$dropped` records all of it,
so a thin claims table can be told apart from a thin literature.

`gr_outline()` then derives the sections from the claims and hands them back as
an ordinary outline you can accept, edit or throw away; `attr(outline, "claims")`
is the assignment of claims to sections. `gr_gaps()` computes what the corpus
does not contain (a declared category nobody studied, a dimension with no
variation, a claim nobody has replicated, a disagreement nothing explains) in R,
with no model call, so the gap list is something you can check by counting:

```{r}
outline <- gr_outline(cm, client = claim_writer)
names(outline)
gr_gaps(cm, extraction = table)[, c("kind", "dimension", "detail")]
```

That outline is one grouping of the claims, and the grouping is the review's
argument. `alternatives = 2` asks for a second, shown the first and asked to
group the claims by a different principle. How far apart two outlines are is
counted, not asked: `distance` is how far each lies from the first, the share of
pairs of claims that one puts together and the other apart. One that groups the
claims as an earlier one did, whatever its headings, is dropped. Nothing ranks
them, and `gr_outline_pick()` hands back the one you choose:

```{r}
two <- gr_outline(cm, client = claim_writer, alternatives = 2)
attr(two, "comparison")[, c("alternative", "sections", "claims_per_section", "distance")]
names(gr_outline_pick(two, 2))
```

Each ends with the closing section for the gaps, which holds no claims here. The
first outline is the same whatever `alternatives` says, and a review written
from a picked one records which it was.

```{r}
from_claims <- gr_synthesise(table, outline = outline, question = protocol$question,
                             client = claim_writer, claims = cm,
                             gaps = gr_gaps(cm, extraction = table))
from_claims$sections[, c("section", "n_claims", "claims_missed", "n_unsupplied", "partial")]
```

The stand-in wrote the same sentence for the gaps section too, citing two
studies that section was not shown, so `n_unsupplied` counts them and the
section is marked partial.

Each section now argues its own claims and is shown only the studies those
claims rest on, ordered so a twelve-person pilot stops getting the same space as
a two-thousand-person trial. `claims_missed` is the citation check run
backwards: a section handed a claim and not writing it up did not do what the
outline promised, is marked partial, and says which claim it left out.
`cite_style = "author-year"` and `coherence = TRUE` work here as they do above.

The schema this wants as input is the `claims` protocol
(`gr_protocols("claims")`). `design` and `finding` are coded as enums so studies
can be compared mechanically, each paired with the paper's own wording so the
coding can be checked rather than trusted. `finding` is coded relative to your
question, which is what lets a non-interventional literature have contradictions
at all, and why that template is refused until you replace the placeholder
question in it.

Two things it does not do. It does not rank study designs when deciding
emphasis: that would assert a cohort study beats a qualitative one, and the
Cochrane Handbook discourages totalling per-item scores into one number. Design
is a grouping variable here, describing what distinguishes the sides of a
disagreement, not a score. And nothing asks a model to judge which of its own
inputs are stale or wrong. If two studies conflict, both are reported and the
conflict is named, because "the model decided this one was wrong" is not
something anyone can check.

## Counting and reporting the run

`gr_flow()` returns the numbers a flow diagram is made of, from what the run
already recorded. Every source is accounted for at every stage it reached, so
the arithmetic closes:

```{r}
gr_flow(screened, table)[, c("stage", "n")]
```

The records screened split into include, exclude, unclear, could not be read
(no screening call was made) and screening call failed (a call was made and its
reply failed or was not the form asked for), and those five rows sum to
"screened". "resolved by a person" counts the decisions a person made with
`gr_resolve()`, "kept for full text" is `$forward`, and "deferred to full text"
is the unclear part of it, `$deferred`. Pass `records =` to start the counts at
identification, and `claims =` to add the claim-level counts.

`gr_audit_report()` writes the whole chain out as one self-contained HTML file
for the reviewer or co-author whose question is "how do you know?". It holds the
protocol as fixed in advance, what happened to every document (the screener's
decision, and who resolved each record, when and why), every value with its
quote and page and whether the quote is there, what was written and which rows
each claim rests on, every claim with the studies for and against it and where
each one ended up, and what it cost. It takes the objects the run already
produced:

```{r eval = FALSE}
gr_audit_report("audit.html", screening = screened, extraction = table,
                synthesis = from_claims, claims = cm, protocol = protocol,
                calibration = cal)
```

`records =` takes the search when the run had one, and every argument is
optional except the path and at least one stage to report on.

The report puts the failures near the top: unverified quotes, documents that
could not be read, screening calls that failed or came back in the wrong form,
and citations pointing at rows that do not exist are counted there. It also
states what the checking does not establish: that a quoted sentence occurs in
the document is not evidence that it supports the value taken from it.

```{r include = FALSE}
gr_options(old)
```
